{{short description|German physicist, professor and author (born 1939)}}
'''Alfred Zehe''' (born May 23, 1939) is a German physicist, professor and author. After American authorities charged him with spying for the [[East Germany|East German]] government in 1983, he became part of a high-profile prisoner exchange between the [[United States|U.S.]] and the [[Soviet Union]].

==Early life and education==
Born in [[Farnstädt]], Germany, Alfred Zehe was trained from a young age to be an underground copper miner. In 1964, he graduated from the [[University of Leipzig]] with a degree in physics; in 1969, he received the degree of Doctor rerum naturalium; and in 1975, he received the degree of Doctor scientiae naturalium.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.cv-az.ece.buap.mx/html/escolaridad.html |title = Escolaridad}}</ref> He held a chair in Experimental Physics at the [[Dresden University of Technology|Technical University of Dresden]] from 1980 to 1991, during which time he taught periodically at the [[Autonomous University of Puebla]] in Puebla, Mexico.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.cv-az.ece.buap.mx/html/puestos_.html |title = Puestos}}</ref> Prior to the 1990 [[German reunification]], Zehe's ability to travel, including his teaching at University of Puebla, was contingent on his consulting with the East German government on matters of national security.<ref name=phoenix/>

==Sting Operation and Arrest==
In 1982, Zehe was summoned from Puebla to the East German embassy in [[Mexico City]] to meet with East German officials, who sought Zehe's expertise regarding recently acquired documents on sonar technology. Unbeknownst to Zehe at the time, the documents had been purchased by East German agents from an undercover U.S. operative in Washington, D.C.<ref name=tfd>Harvey A. Silverglate, ''Three Felonies a Day: How the Feds Target the Innocent'' (Encounter Books, 2009), 219</ref>

The U.S. operative, in an [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]]-managed sting operation, had gone shopping on Washington's embassy row "to lure a spy from one or another of the Communist embassies to come out and take the bait."<ref name=spytrader>Craig R. Whitney, ''Spy Trader: The Darkest Secrets of the Cold War'' (Random House, 1993), 266</ref> After purchasing the documents, the East Germans realized they lacked the expertise in Washington to evaluate the intelligence, so they called on Zehe in Mexico City. There, he reviewed the documents, which turned out to be outdated information on submarine sonar-detection, and returned to his teaching post in Puebla.<ref name=tfd/>

On November 3, 1983, Zehe was arrested while attending the annual symposium of the [[American Vacuum Society]] in Boston.<ref name=nytplea>''New York Times'': [https://www.nytimes.com/1985/02/22/us/east-german-enters-guilty-plea-to-buying-secret-us-documents.html "East German Enters Guilty Plea to Buying Secret U.S. Documents," February 25, 1985], accessed December 8, 2010</ref> He was subsequently charged under the [[Espionage Act of 1917|Espionage Act]] with conspiracy to obtain classified documents related to military technology and deliver them to a foreign government.<ref name=nytplea/>

The decision to arrest him at the conference with television cameras on hand was designed to fuel public awareness of the dangers of scientific espionage.<ref name=redhead>P. A. Redhead, ed., ''Vacuum Science and Technology: Pioneers of the 20th Century'', History of Vacuum Science and Technology, vol. 2 (American Vacuum Society, 1994), 21</ref>

The [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]] later asked the American Vacuum Society to furnish it with the names of the 2600 attendees at the Boston meeting and threatened to subpoena the information. The Society declined but replied that it would comply with such a subpoena. The FBI did not pursue the matter.<ref>Mitchel B. Wallerstein, Lawrence E. McCray, ''Scientific Communication and National Security: The Issues in 1984'', January 31, 1984, 11, [https://books.google.com/books?id=IEMrAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA11& available online], accessed December 8, 2010</ref>

The East German government posted [[bail]] for Zehe in June 1984.<ref name=nytplea/> He remained in Boston while awaiting trial.<ref name=redhead/>

[[Wolfgang Vogel]], East German lawyer and spy trader, was enlisted by the East German government to help free Zehe.<ref>''Berliner Zeitung'': [http://www.berlinonline.de/berliner-zeitung/archiv/.bin/dump.fcgi/1995/0612/reporter/0025/index.html Andreas Förster, "Der Regisseur fuhr im goldfarbenen Mercedes vor," June 12, 1995] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100614064509/http://www.berlinonline.de/berliner-zeitung/archiv/.bin/dump.fcgi/1995/0612/reporter/0025/index.html |date=June 14, 2010 }}, accessed December 8, 2010</ref> Vogel contacted [[Alan Dershowitz]] to oversee the legal aspects of the effort and [[Ronald Greenwald]] to act as personal liaison between him and Zehe.<ref name=spytrader/> Dershowitz, seeking to avoid a [[conflict of interest]] with his then-client [[Natan Sharansky|Anatoly Shcharansky]], a founder of the Refusenik movement who had been imprisoned in Moscow for allegedly spying for the United States, brought in [[Harvey A. Silverglate]] to defend Zehe.<ref>''Spy Trader'', 265</ref>

Silverglate claimed that under any reasonable interpretation of the Espionage Act, Zehe had not committed a crime.<ref>''Three Felonies a Day'', 220</ref> Zehe did not purchase the documents at issue in the case, but only reviewed documents presented to him in Mexico City, Silverglate asserted. He also told how at [[Robert Mueller]]'s direction, prosecutors used "national security" as a reason to withhold documents from the defense even though they were prepared to let the East Germans review them.<ref name=phoenix/> Silverglate further contended that the indictment was invalid because the Espionage Act does not cover espionage conducted by a foreign citizen outside the United States.<ref name=nytplea/>

On January 29, 1985, U.S. District Judge David S. Nelson denied Zehe's motion to dismiss the case, ruling that the Espionage Act could be applied [[Extraterritoriality|extraterritorially]] to both citizens and noncitizens because of the threat to national security that espionage poses.<ref>United States v. Zehe, 601 F.Supp. 196 (D. Mass 1985); Kent College of Law: [http://www.kentlaw.edu/faculty/rwarner/classes/carter/2008_lectures/2008_cases/zehe.doc United States v. Zehe, January 29, 1985], accessed December 8, 2010</ref>

U.S. prosecutors then offered to allow Zehe to defect to the United States, where he could take residence and continue his academic career.<ref name=tfd222>''Three Felonies a Day'', 222</ref> Despite being closely watched by the East German government, Zehe accepted this offer and agreed to defect. Shortly thereafter, however, the U.S. government refused to accept Zehe as a bona fide defector.<ref name=tfd222/> He was left with the option of either pleading guilty and hoping for a light sentence, or pleading not-guilty and testing the American legal system.

On February 25, 1985, Zehe entered a plea of guilty.<ref name=nytplea/> He submitted to a full debriefing in exchange for the promise of a light sentence. He was sentenced to 8 years in prison.<ref name=nytfree/>

==Prisoner Exchange==
Zehe was released in June 1985 as part of an exchange of four East Europeans held by the U.S. for 25 people held in Poland and East Germany, none of them American.<ref name=nytfree>''New York Times'': [https://www.nytimes.com/1985/06/16/weekinreview/the-world-free-to-spy-another-day.html? Milt Freudenheim and Henry Giniger, "Free to Spy Another Day?," June 16, 1985], accessed December 8, 2010</ref> The exchange took place on the [[Glienicke Bridge]] linking [[West Berlin]] with [[Potsdam]], [[East Germany]].<ref>''Los Angeles Times'': [https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-06-11-mn-10338-story.html "U.S. Swaps 4 Red Spies for 25 Held as Western Agents," June 11, 1985], accessed December 8, 2010</ref>

Silverglate used Zehe's case to argue against the 2001 appointment of [[Robert Mueller]] to head the FBI.<ref name=phoenix>''Boston Phoenix'': [http://www.bostonphoenix.com/boston/news_features/this_just_in/documents/01710021.htm Harvey A. Silverglate, "Freedom Watch: The Real Bob Mueller," July 12-19, 2001] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120614083149/http://www.bostonphoenix.com/boston/news_features/this_just_in/documents/01710021.htm |date=2012-06-14 }}, accessed December 8, 2010</ref> On another occasion, Silverglate argued that the FBI was trying to acquire assets it could trade with Eastern European governments, part of what he termed "spy trading culture."<ref>''Forbes'': [https://web.archive.org/web/20121103041956/http://www.forbes.com/2010/07/15/russian-spies-espionage-cia-opinions-columnists-harvey-a-silverglate_2.html "Subversive Suburbanites," July 15, 2010], accessed December 8, 2010</ref>

==Academic career==
In his academic career, Zehe's major research fields have been [[materials science]], [[solid-state electronics]], and vacuum physics. He is the author of ''Tecnologia epitaxial de silicio'' (2001 with Andreas Thomas)<ref>COSIS.net Bookshop: [http://shop.cosis.net/bookstore/book/379882/0/COST/BOK/EN9783831114382/Alfred_Zehe__Andreas_Thomas__Tecnologia_epitaxial_de_silicio.htmlTecnologia epitaxial de silicio] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110723054731/http://shop.cosis.net/bookstore/book/379882/0/COST/BOK/EN9783831114382/Alfred_Zehe__Andreas_Thomas__Tecnologia_epitaxial_de_silicio.htmlTecnologia |date=2011-07-23 }}, accessed December 8, 2010</ref> and ''Herramientas Analiticas de Interfaces Solidas'' (2002).<ref>COSIS.net Bookshop: [http://shop.cosis.net/bookstore/book/380766/0/COST/BOK/EN9783831132621/A__Zehe__Herramientas__Analiticas_de_Interfaces_Solidas.html Herramientas Analiticas de Interfaces Solidas] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110723055853/http://shop.cosis.net/bookstore/book/380766/0/COST/BOK/EN9783831132621/A__Zehe__Herramientas__Analiticas_de_Interfaces_Solidas.html |date=2011-07-23 }}, accessed December 8, 2010</ref>
